units.translation: These are read in M: ἀζην ίουσ ίώ [with the accents erased] | μῆνις μάστειρ᾽ ἐκ θεῶν [the wrath, a scourge from the gods], on which the scholiast says: ὦ Ζεῦ, ἡ παρὰ τῶν θεῶν μῆνις κατὰ Ἰοῦς ὠδῆς ἐστι καὶ μαστιγωτική [O Zeus, the wrath from the gods against Io is of song and of scourging]. From these the reading ἃ Ζὴν Ἰοῦς has been rightly restored, which is the ancient form of the name Ζεύς [Zeus] (Doric Záv in Arist. Av. 570, which Bamberger wanted to restore also in Aeschylus; Bernhardy changed it to Ζῆν ' in his book on syntax p. 134), about which I have spoken in Thes. vol. 4 p. 22. But the emendation of the letters iw is uncertain, which cannot signify the interjection iú, alien to this place: for this reason Hermann wrote iῷ and changed ὠδῆς in the scholiast's words to ἰώδης, taking both as said of anger, which is not approved by the example he adduces, Ag. 834 δύσφρων γὰρ ἰὸς καρδίαν προσήμενος [for a hostile poison sits upon the heart]. Nor does ἰώδης ever have the meaning of irascible, but of rusty or poisonous. Therefore Wecklein's conjecture is better (in Philologus vol. 32 p. 185) that ὠδῆς is corrupted from μανιώδης, although this is perhaps the interpreter's word, not Aeschylus's, who used some more exquisite word, such as οἰστρώδης, as οἶστρος is explained by μανία by the grammarians, unless this very word is to be restored for ὠδῆς in the scholiast, as Io below v. 541 is called οἴστρῳ ἐρεσσομένα [driven by the gadfly], in Pr. 682 and in Sophocles El. 2 οἰστροπλήξ [stung by the gadfly], and the remaining words compounded with οἶστρος, mentioned in Thes. vol. 5 p. 1837, in interpreting all of which the grammarians use the word μανίας. Furthermore μάστειρ ' is suspect, which since the scholiast explains by μαστιγωτική, he seems to have read μαστίκτειρ᾽, as Hartung observed, from the masculine μαστίκτωρ, which Aeschylus used in Eum. 160, or μαστικτήρ, which Auratus restored for μακιστῆρα in Suppl. 466. The whole passage therefore seems to be written thus: ἃ Ζὴν, Ἰοῦς οἰστρώδης | μῆνις μαστίκτειρ᾽ ἐκ θεῶν [O Zeus, the gadfly-like wrath, a scourge from the gods] (θεῶν as one syllable). | κοννώ δ᾽ ἄταν γαμετᾶς σᾶς [and the ruin of your marriage] (σᾶς added by Hermann) | οὐρανόνικον [conquering heaven] (in M γαμετουρανόνεικον, from which Turnebus made γαμετᾶς οὐρανανίκου, to which Aeschylus seems to have preferred the accusative οὐρανόνικον because of the nearby genitive χαλεποῦ) · χαλεποῦ γὰρ ἐκ πνεύματος εἰσι χειμών [for from a harsh wind comes a storm]. On Io's madness compare the choral song v. 540 ff. The scholiast rightly notes that the next strophe of the chorus, v. 168 καὶ τότ᾽ καλούμενος [and then being called], coheres with the previous strophe ending at v. 161. For verses 162-167, which Canterus understood should be repeated after v. 172, are intercalary, as above 141-143 = 151-153: to which the scholiast's annotation points, written thus in M without a lemma: τὴν τῆς Ἥρας τῆς ἐν ἀνδρείᾳ νικώσης πάντας τοὺς ἐν οὐρανῷ θεούς. καὶ ἐφ᾽ ἡμᾶς οὖν ἔφθασεν ἡ μῆνις τῆς Ἥρας. πρὸς τὸ ἄνω τοῦτο “τὸν πολυξενώτατον Ζῆνα τῶν κεκμηκότων ἱξόμεσθα” χαλεποῦ γὰρ ἐκ πνεύμα-τος εἶσι χειμών. τὰ δ᾽ ἄλλα διὰ μέσου ἀναπεφώνηται. [the wrath of Hera, who in manliness conquers all the gods in heaven. And so the wrath of Hera has come upon us. In reference to the above: "we shall come to Zeus, most hospitable to the dead," for from a harsh wind comes a storm. The rest has been uttered in between.] These have coalesced from two annotations.
